notes.meaning: Solomon started building the Lord's temple on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem. This was the threshing floor David bought from Ornan after God stopped a deadly plague there. Ancient Jewish tradition also saw this mountain as the very place where Abraham offered up his son Isaac.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars question whether this hill is the exact same site as the land of Moriah in Genesis, since older biblical narratives do not explicitly connect the two events.

notes.meaning: Solomon began the building project on the second day of the second month, during the fourth year of his reign. He spent his early years gathering materials and organizing workers before laying the first stones. His careful preparation showed how deeply he valued God's house.

Solomon laid the foundation of the temple sixty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, which is about ninety feet long and thirty feet wide. These measurements followed the older, sacred standard handed down from the days of Moses. David had also given Solomon these building plans guided by God's Spirit.

The entrance hall, or porch, extended across the entire front of the temple, measuring twenty cubits wide. Solomon covered the inside walls of this entryway with pure gold to welcome worshippers with royal splendor.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: While the standard Hebrew text records the porch height as 120 cubits, most ancient translations and modern scholars read twenty cubits, seeing 120 as an early copying error.

notes.meaning: Solomon lined the main hall with cypress wood panels and overlaid them with fine gold. He carved images of palm trees and chains into the wood, filling the sacred hall with symbols of life, fruitfulness, and beauty.

The walls and floors were adorned with beautiful, valuable stones alongside pure gold brought from Parvaim. Parvaim was an ancient region famous for producing gold of the highest quality. Solomon spared no expense in dedicating the best of the earth to God.

Every beam, doorway, wall, and door inside the room was overlaid with pure gold, and figures of cherubim were carved throughout. Cherubim are mighty angelic beings who dwell in God's presence. These carvings reminded the priests that earthly worship joins with the praise of heaven.

Solomon constructed the Most Holy Place, the inner room where God's special presence dwelt, as an exact cube measuring twenty cubits on each side. He covered its walls with six hundred talents of fine gold, which was an enormous fortune. This room was set apart as the sacred resting place for the Ark of the Covenant.

Even the nails used to secure the gold sheets were made of solid gold, each weighing fifty shekels, or well over a pound. The upper chambers above the main ceiling were also coated in gold. Every hidden corner was treated with the same reverence as the visible rooms.

Inside the Most Holy Place, Solomon placed two large sculptured figures of cherubim and overlaid them with gold. Unlike the smaller cherubim attached to the ark in the desert tent, these were giant standing figures. They served as majestic guardians over God's footstool.

Each cherub had two wings measuring five cubits each, giving them a combined wingspan of twenty cubits across the room. One wing of each cherub touched an outer wall, while their inner wings met and touched in the middle. Together, their outstretched wings spanned the entire width of the Most Holy Place.

The two cherubim stood on their feet with their wings fully spread, facing forward toward the main hall. Rather than facing each other, they stood like attendants looking out into the room. Their standing posture portrayed ready servants waiting on the Lord.

Solomon made a thick curtain using rich blue, purple, and crimson yarn and fine linen, with cherubim woven into the cloth. This veil hung between the main hall and the Most Holy Place to shield people from God's holy presence. When Jesus died on the cross, this temple veil tore open, giving all believers direct access to God.

Solomon set two large bronze pillars in front of the temple entrance, topped with ornate capitals measuring five cubits high. Standing by the porch, they welcomed everyone who came near to worship the Lord.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The height of thirty-five cubits is commonly understood as the combined length of both pillars, because other biblical books record each pillar as eighteen cubits tall.

notes.meaning: Interwoven bronze chains were placed on top of the pillars, and one hundred decorative pomegranates were fastened onto each set of chains. Pomegranates were well-known symbols of blessing, life, and fruitfulness in Israel.

Solomon set up the pillars at the entrance, naming the southern one Jachin and the northern one Boaz. Jachin means 'He will establish,' and Boaz means 'in Him is strength.' Whenever worshippers entered the temple gates, these names reminded them that God alone establishes and strengthens His people.
